title: Run an under-sink reverse osmosis filter on 12 or 24 V
summary: A salvaged under-sink reverse osmosis unit fed by a 12 or 24 V booster pump takes salt, nitrate and metals out of well or surface water for roughly 2 to 20 watt-hours a litre. It sends several litres down the drain for each litre it makes, needs clear, chlorine-free feed, can lose its flow for good if the membrane dries out after use, does not reliably remove fuel or solvents, and does not replace disinfecting: Pentair says to disinfect, and DuPont says its element alone doesn't guarantee germ removal.

materials.item: Under-sink RO unit: pre-filter housings, membrane housing and membrane, storage tank, shut-off valve, check valve and drain flow restrictor
12 or 24 V DC diaphragm booster pump made for RO (an RO boost pump)
Tank pressure switch to stop the pump when the tank is full (pumped units have one)
12 V battery, or the 24 V supply from a pumped unit, with an inline fuse at the battery
Fuse and holder sized for the pump's wire
Fresh sediment and carbon pre-filter cartridges
1/4 in food-grade tubing and push-fit fittings
Covered feed tank or food-grade bucket, and a second container for the reject water
TDS meter, to compare feed and product water
Plain unscented household bleach, for sanitising the housings and treating the product water

steps.text: Decide whether RO is worth it. It is for salty or hard water and for nitrate (AHS nitrate). For germs alone, boiling or chlorine is simpler, and Pentair says to disinfect RO water before or after the unit, while DuPont says its element alone doesn't guarantee germ removal (Pentair RO-2550, DuPont TW30).

Check the feed. Check the rating on your unit. Pentair's is rated for up to 2,000 ppm dissolved solids, 10 grains (171 mg/L) of hardness and pH 3–11 (Pentair RO-2550). USGS calls 1,000–3,000 ppm slightly saline and 10,000–35,000 ppm highly saline (USGS saline), so Pentair's 2,000 ppm rating is well short of highly saline water.

Judge the salvaged membrane. One that was used and then dried out may have lost its flow for good (DuPont manual). One still dry and sealed in its factory bag is made for a long shelf life (DuPont TW30, DuPont manual). A membrane that came wet in its bag holds a preservative (DuPont's is 1 % food-grade sodium metabisulfite): wear gloves and eye protection when you handle it (DuPont manual).

Check the housings and tank for cracks, especially after a freeze: Pentair says freezing can crack the filter and cause leaks (Pentair RO-2550), so replace any cartridge or housing that froze, whether or not it looks cracked. Replace clear housing bowls older than 5 years and opaque ones older than 10 (Pentair RO-2550). Sanitise the empty housings now, before you fit the cartridges and membrane: the method is in the last step.

Fit fresh sediment and carbon pre-filters. The carbon takes chlorine out before the membrane, which tolerates less than 0.1 ppm of free chlorine (DuPont TW30). With chlorinated or periodically chlorinated water Pentair says a carbon pre-filter is absolutely necessary, to be changed at least every 3 months, and suggests checking the drain water with a chlorine test kit: none should show (Pentair RO-2550).
steps.warn: Never feed chlorinated or bleach-treated water straight to the membrane: free chlorine destroys it over time (DuPont manual).

steps.text: Plumb the pump into the feed line ahead of the membrane, with the sediment filter ahead of the pump. Keep the drain flow restrictor that came with the membrane (Pentair lists one matched to its membrane) (Pentair RO-2550).

Wire the pump through the tank's pressure switch and an inline fuse at the battery, so it stops when the tank is full. With no pressure switch, run it only while you are there to watch it, and switch it off the moment the tank is full: the unit stops making water then (Pentair RO-2550), and a pump pushing against a closed line builds pressure.
steps.warn: Fuse the positive lead close to the battery, as in [DC wiring](#guides/skill_dc_wiring).

steps.text: Aim for 40–100 psi (2.75–6.9 bar) at the membrane, the range Pentair gives for its unit (Pentair RO-2550). Aquatec's 8800 RO pumps give their rated flow at up to 80 psi, and their data sheets list a by-pass relief setting for each pressure, from 30 to 110 psi (Aquatec 12 V, Aquatec 24 V). The 110 psi setting is above Pentair's 100 psi limit, so check a salvaged pump's setting against your unit's limit, and never run past what the housings and fittings are rated for.
Check every joint for leaks each hour for the first 3 hours: leaks can appear only once pressure has built (Pentair RO-2550). Keep the pump, battery and wiring above and clear of the water joints.

Run the reject (drain) line into a container, not away. Several litres go to drain for each litre made (Pentair RO-2550, EPA WaterSense RO); use it for flushing toilets or cleaning, never for drinking: it carries what the membrane held back (Pentair RO-2550).

Flush a new or restarted membrane: throw away what it makes in the first hour (DuPont TW30), and drain the first full tank, or more, to clear carbon dust from the post-filter: Pentair's own start-up drains it five times (Pentair RO-2550).

Test with a TDS meter: product water should read a small fraction of the feed. Pentair's unit is rated at 95 % rejection (Pentair RO-2550). Pentair says product at about 30 % or more of the feed's TDS means the membrane may need replacing or the drain flow tubing may be clogged (Pentair RO-2550).

Disinfect the product water before drinking, by boiling or plain unscented bleach, as Pentair's warning says (Pentair RO-2550). If the feed was high in nitrate, use bleach: boiling raises nitrate (AHS nitrate). Take the dose, and the longer contact time for cold water, from [Test bleach strength](#guides/test_bleach_strength), then check free chlorine as in [Test water](#guides/test_water).

Never let it freeze or dry out. Keep the unit and feed inside the warm part of the house. Pentair says to empty the tank if the unit sits 2–3 days, and DuPont says that after 48 hours down a system must not dry out and needs flushing every 24 hours or a preservative (Pentair RO-2550, DuPont manual).
steps.warn: If it must stand longer, take the membrane out, seal it in a plastic bag and keep it in a fridge, never frozen (Pentair RO-2550). DuPont soaks a used element in 1 % sodium metabisulfite before bagging it (DuPont manual).

steps.text: Sanitise the housings before a salvaged unit is first run, and each time you change the membrane. With the old membrane and the cartridges out, fill each housing about one third with water, add 2 tablespoons of plain unscented household bleach and screw it back on. Run the cold feed for 2–3 minutes, let it stand 30 minutes, run it out for 3–5 minutes, then discard the bleach water, rinse, and fit the new membrane and cartridges (Pentair RO-2550).
steps.warn: Never mix bleach with acid descalers or other cleaners. Wear gloves and eye protection, and keep bleach water off the membrane: chlorine ruins it (DuPont manual).

notes:
## What reverse osmosis does
Pressure pushes water through a membrane that holds back dissolved salts and minerals; what's held back goes to drain as reject water (Pentair RO-2550). A home membrane takes out about 99 % of salt at its test point (DuPont TW30), and a whole under-sink unit is rated lower: Pentair's at 95 % (Pentair RO-2550). It's the household answer to salty or hard well water and to dissolved salts, nitrate and metals that boiling can't touch. It does not take out everything: UNL says some pesticides, solvents and volatile organic chemicals are not removed by RO, and hydrogen sulphide passes through, so water with fuel or solvent in it needs a different source (UNL RO). For nitrate above Canada's limit of 45 mg/L, Alberta Health Services recommends a point-of-use RO unit certified to NSF/ANSI 58, or a distiller; at very high levels, such as 100 mg/L nitrate-nitrogen, RO might not remove enough (AHS nitrate). See [Water filters](#guides/reference_water_filters) for how RO compares with carbon, UV and the rest.

**Germs:** a membrane can stop germs, but the makers don't promise it. DuPont says its element on its own doesn't guarantee removal of cysts and pathogens, which depends on the whole system and its upkeep (DuPont TW30). Pentair's manual says its unit won't protect against disease-causing bacteria, and not to use it on water that is unsafe or of unknown quality without disinfection before or after (Pentair RO-2550). A salvaged unit with tired O-rings is exactly that case. **Clear, RO, then boil or chlorinate.** If the feed was high in nitrate, chlorinate rather than boil: boiling raises nitrate, and babies under 3 months are most at risk from nitrate, including in formula (AHS nitrate). UNL says to feed an RO unit coliform-free water, because bacteria can damage the membrane and pinholes let germs through (UNL RO).

## Is it worth the power?
| Method | Energy per litre | Source |
|---|---|---|
| RO with a 12 V booster pump | About 2–20 Wh (worked below) | Aquatec 12 V, DuPont TW30, Pentair RO-2550 |
| Distilling on electricity | About 1 kWh | [Distil water on a stove](#guides/build_water_still) |

Aquatec's 12 V RO pump draws about 1.0–1.7 A at 60–80 psi, so 12–20 W (Aquatec 12 V). Worked out:
- **Best case:** a bare 50 GPD membrane makes about 7.9 L an hour at its 50 psi, 25 °C test point (DuPont TW30): about 2 Wh per litre.
- **A whole unit:** Pentair rates its 4-stage unit at 43.6 L a day (Pentair RO-2550), under 2 L an hour: about 10 Wh per litre if the pump runs the whole time.
- **Cold winter feed:** at 10 °C the membrane gives about 58 % of that (DuPont manual): up to about 20 Wh per litre.

So RO costs roughly 2–20 Wh a litre, against about 1,000 Wh to distil one. When the water is salty, RO wins by a mile. When it only needs germs killed, it's wasted effort.

Honest output from a whole unit is modest: Pentair's is rated at 43.6 L (11.5 US gal) a day, and it needs about 2–4 hours to refill its 10.6 L tank, drop by drop (Pentair RO-2550). RO water is also more corrosive than untreated water (UNL RO), so keep it in plastic tubing and food-grade containers rather than old brass, copper or soldered parts (that last advice is our inference). Plan on drinking and cooking water, not washing water.

## Cold water
Output falls as the water cools. By DuPont's temperature correction, a membrane at 10 °C gives about 58 % of its 25 °C flow, and at 15 °C about 70 % (DuPont manual). Pentair's unit is rated for feed from 4.4 to 37.7 °C (40–100 °F) (Pentair RO-2550). Winter well water is near the bottom of that range, and meltwater, close to 0 °C, is below it, so keep the feed tank in the warm house. Don't heat it past the unit's own limit: 37.7 °C for Pentair's unit (Pentair RO-2550), 45 °C for the DuPont element (DuPont TW30).

## Pressure and the pump
- **How much:** Pentair wants 40–100 psi (2.75–6.9 bar) of feed (Pentair RO-2550). DuPont tests its 50 GPD element at 50 psi (3.4 bar) and allows up to 150 psi (10 bar) (DuPont TW30). A tank a metre above the unit gives only about 0.1 bar (1.4 psi), which is why off-grid RO needs a pump.
- **Which pump:** RO boost pumps are small diaphragm pumps. Aquatec's 8800 series comes in 12 V and 24 V DC versions, primes itself from 1.2–2.1 m (4–7 ft) below, can run dry, and gives about 0.7–1.5 L a minute at 80 psi depending on the pump head (Aquatec 12 V, Aquatec 24 V). Its inlet must not see more than 60 psi (Aquatec 12 V).
- **Duty:** Aquatec rates these pumps to run continuously at their listed pressures, but says to run them only as needed to save the wearing parts (Aquatec 12 V). A tank pressure switch does that for you.
- **Where to find one:** pumped under-sink units ([RO system](#browse/devices/ro_system)), and [water vending machines](#browse/devices/water_vending), which run bigger membranes and pumps of their own.

## Reject water
The drain stream carries away what the membrane held back. EPA says a typical system wastes 5 US gal or more for every gallon made, some up to 10; units with the WaterSense label waste 2.3 or less (EPA WaterSense RO). Pentair just says several gallons per gallon (Pentair RO-2550). The split between product and reject is set by the valve or restrictor on the reject line (DuPont manual); under-sink units use a fixed flow restrictor matched to the membrane (Pentair RO-2550). Don't pinch the reject down to waste less: the more of the feed you push through as product (the recovery), the worse the membrane holds back salt, and plants set recovery to stop salts crystallising inside the membrane (DuPont manual). Catch the reject instead: it carries what the membrane held back, so use it for flushing toilets and cleaning, not for drinking, washing hands or dishes, or food crops; from salty water it's saltier than the feed (Pentair RO-2550).

## Pre-filters and the membrane's enemies
- **Chlorine:** the membrane tolerates less than 0.1 ppm (DuPont TW30); 1 ppm for 200–1,000 hours can wear it out (DuPont manual). The carbon pre-filter is what stops it. If you chlorinate stored water, run it through carbon before the RO, and chlorinate again after.
- **Hardness and iron:** above 10 grains (171 mg/L) hardness, scale builds fast and plugs the membrane (Pentair RO-2550). Keep iron, manganese and sulphide very low (Pentair RO-2550).
- **Grit:** the sediment filter keeps it off the pump and membrane. Change pre-filters when flow drops; Pentair's schedule is every six months for the pre-filters (every three months for the carbon pre-filter on chlorinated water) and twelve for the post-filter (Pentair RO-2550).
- **Drying:** a used membrane that dries out may lose its flow for good (DuPont manual). New elements shipped dry are fine until wetted (DuPont manual).
- **Freezing:** Pentair says freezing can crack the filter and cause leaks, and never to freeze a membrane in storage (Pentair RO-2550). DuPont's no-damage statement is for elements being shipped, dry or in preservative, and thawed before use (DuPont manual); that isn't the same as a wet membrane that froze in a working unit. Treat anything that froze in service as suspect, as the filter-check card does ([Check a found or frozen water filter](#guides/test_water_filter)): replace the cartridges and housings that froze, check the product with a TDS meter, and disinfect it anyway.

## Lay-up
DuPont's rule for big plants is useful at home: a system can stop for 24 hours without precautions, but longer than 48 hours it must not dry out and needs flushing every 24 hours or chemical preservation (DuPont manual). Pentair's home version: empty the tank if unused 2–3 days, flush for 5 minutes after time off, and for long stops seal the membrane in a bag in the fridge, never frozen (Pentair RO-2550).
